vignette:
Catalina's Wound

Catalina was twenty-three when the men came to her apartment in San Pedro Sula. She had been working as an apprentice electrician then, still learning the trade, still believing that hard work and keeping her head down would keep her safe. She was alone—her roommate had gone home for the weekend—when they knocked. She remembers the sound of her own voice saying yes when they asked if she was Catalina Mendez. She remembers the moment she understood they were not there about a debt or a job. She remembers the woman among them, the one who smiled while the others held her down, the one who asked questions in a voice that never rose, never wavered. For four hours, Catalina was not free to leave. The door was locked from the outside. There were three of them, and she was one. When it was over, she could not say why they had come or what they wanted her to know. She only knew that she had been chosen, and that the woman's presence had made it worse—had made it feel personal in a way she could not articulate.

She left Honduras three months later with a tourist visa and $800. She did not return.

Now, at twenty-seven, Catalina works as an HVAC technician in Phoenix, installing and servicing heating systems in residential and commercial buildings. It is skilled work, respected work, work that pays steadily. But in the four years since she came to the United States, something has fractured inside her that no amount of competence can repair. She cannot be alone in a closed space with another woman without her chest tightening, without her mind cataloging exits and calculating whether she could reach the door. Last month, a female supervisor came to observe her work in a basement utility room—a routine quality check—and Catalina found herself unable to breathe. She had to tell her supervisor she was ill and leave the job site early. The supervisor had not seemed angry, but Catalina was certain she had lost respect, that she had revealed something broken that could never be hidden again.

At night, Catalina lies awake listening. She checks the locks on her apartment door and windows—first at midnight, then at two, then at four. Sometimes she checks six or seven times before dawn. When she does sleep, she wakes suddenly, her body rigid, her first thought always where is the door? She startles at small sounds: a neighbor's television through the wall, a car alarm two blocks away, the hum of the refrigerator shifting into a new cycle. Her hands shake sometimes when she is holding tools, and she has learned to grip harder, to press her palms against her thighs until the tremor passes.

When the memory comes—and it comes without warning, triggered by a woman's voice in a grocery store, by the sight of someone with a bandage on their hand, by the feeling of being trapped in traffic with no way out—Catalina feels a shame so profound that it seems to originate from a place deeper than her body. She is ashamed that she could not stop it. She is ashamed that she is still afraid. She is ashamed most of all that she cannot trust herself anymore, that the person she was before—capable, steady, certain of her own judgment—is gone. When the memory fully surfaces, the emotion is so overwhelming that she has to stop whatever she is doing. She has pulled her truck over on the highway. She has walked out of supply stores. She has sat on the floor of her bathroom with the shower running, unable to move until the wave passes.

What frightens Catalina most is not that it might happen again. It is that she has already been permanently changed, that she will never again be the woman who could work confidently in any space, who could trust her own instincts, who could look another person in the eye without calculating risk. She came to her first therapy appointment because her supervisor—the same woman from the basement—had gently suggested that Catalina might benefit from talking to someone. Catalina agreed because she is running out of excuses, because the checking and the waking and the trembling have become the architecture of her life, and because some small part of her, the part that still remembers what it felt like to feel safe, is still hoping that part of herself might be salvageable.
